content.title: About
content.content: Clams are marine bivalve mollusks that are most commonly prepared by steaming or boiling. They have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a tender, slightly chewy texture. Clams are enjoyed as a snack, added to soups, pastas, risottos, and seafood salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Clams filter water, removing microscopic particles and bacteria, effectively cleaning their environment.
There are over 3,000 species of clams, but the blue mussel (Mytilus edulis) and the Mediterranean mussel (Mytilus galloprovincialis) are the most widely used in cuisine.
Clams can grow quickly; some species reach market size in just 6–8 weeks.
In ancient cultures clams were used as bio‑indicators of water quality – their absence could signal pollution.
Clams are considered one of the most sustainable seafood options because their farming requires minimal resources.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Clams provide about 10–12 g of protein per 100 g, offering a high‑quality animal protein source.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: They contain less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, most of which are polyunsaturated.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for blood formation and nerve function; clams supply over 100 % of the daily value per 100 g.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function, metabolism, and skin health.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Clams provide modest amounts of EPA and DHA, which benefit cardiovascular health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Toxin contamination
items.content: Clams can accumulate toxins such as domoic acid when harvested from polluted waters; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: While moderate, cholesterol in clams should be considered by those with hypercholesterolemia.

items.title: Raw consumption risk
items.content: Eating raw clams increases the risk of foodborne illness; always cook until shells fully open.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steam clams for 5–7 minutes or boil them for 3–5 minutes until the shells open. Serve with lemon, garlic butter, soy sauce, or add to pasta, risotto, soups, and seafood salads. Remember to discard any unopened shells and rinse the clams to remove sand.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep live clams in the refrigerator in a container covered with a damp cloth for no more than 24 hours. Frozen clams should be stored in an airtight bag for up to 3 months. Rinse thoroughly under cold running water before cooking.
